Origen of Alexandria
OR-uh-jen of al-EX-an-dree-uh
proper noun (church history / patristics / allegorical hermeneutics)
Greek Origén&275;s (Οριγένης), possibly meaning “born of Horus” (the Egyptian deity) — a pagan name given in the cultural context of Alexandria; also known as Origen Adamantius (“man of steel”); born in Alexandria circa 185 AD; son of Christian parents; his father Leonidas was martyred circa 202 AD under Septimius Severus; Origen headed the Alexandrian catechetical school from approximately 202–231 AD; later established a school at Caesarea Maritima; died circa 254 AD from injuries sustained during the Decian persecution

Biblical Definition

Origen of Alexandria is the most brilliant and most controversial theologian of the third century: the founder of systematic biblical commentary, the first theologian to apply philosophical precision to the entire range of Christian doctrine, and a deeply flawed teacher whose errors were eventually condemned. His genuine contributions were enormous: he produced the Hexapla, a six-column comparative edition of the Old Testament texts; he wrote the first major systematic theology (On First Principles, De Principiis); and his biblical commentaries on nearly every book of Scripture remained authoritative reference works for centuries. His hermeneutical method was the problem: his allegorical approach to Scripture (derived partly from Philo of Alexandria) allowed him to spiritualize texts whose literal sense was theologically inconvenient and to develop speculative doctrines unsupported by the biblical text. His most consequential errors include: the pre-existence of souls (all rational beings existed before creation as mind-spirits), universal restoration (apokatastasis — that all creatures, including the devil, will ultimately be saved), and a Christology that subordinated the Son to the Father in ways that anticipated Arianism. The Fifth Ecumenical Council (Constantinople II, 553 AD) anathematized Origenism. He is the textbook case of brilliant intellect outrunning apostolic tradition, and the Reformed tradition's caution about speculative theology is partly rooted in this example.

Webster 1828 Definition

ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA: third-century Alexandrian theologian and biblical scholar (c. 185–254 AD); founder of systematic biblical commentary and producer of the Hexapla; his allegorical hermeneutic produced brilliant insights and dangerous errors including pre-existence of souls, universal restoration (apokatastasis), and subordinationism; condemned by the Fifth Ecumenical Council (553 AD).

ORIGEN. n. [Gr. Origén&275;s.] Origen Adamantius; born Alexandria, Egypt, c. 185 AD; head of the Alexandrian catechetical school (c. 202–231 AD); prolific biblical commentator and systematic theologian; died c. 254 AD at Tyre from injuries sustained during the Decian persecution.

The Hexapla: Origen's monumental six-column comparison of Old Testament texts (Hebrew, Hebrew in Greek letters, Aquila's Greek translation, Symmachus's, the LXX with marks, Theodotion's translation), the most extensive textual-critical work on the Old Testament in antiquity. His textual scholarship at this level was genuine and lasting.

De Principiis (On First Principles, c. 220–230 AD): the first systematic Christian theology, covering God, Christ, the Spirit, the soul, and Scripture. Its speculative reach exceeded what Scripture teaches: the pre-existence of souls, a graduated hierarchy of rational beings, the possibility of universal restoration. These speculations were not exegetically grounded but philosophically derived.

Hermeneutical method: Origen taught three senses of Scripture — literal, moral, and allegorical — with the allegorical as the highest and most spiritually significant. This allowed him to bypass texts whose literal sense seemed unworthy of God and to generate theological content from the allegorical meaning he constructed. The Reformed tradition has rejected this method as opening Scripture to the interpreter's imagination rather than the text's control.

Anathema at Constantinople II (553 AD): the council condemned fifteen Origenist propositions, including the pre-existence of souls, the spherical form of resurrected bodies, and the restoration of demons and the devil. The condemnation came three centuries after Origen's death and targeted a developed Origenism among his followers rather than Origen himself, but the core speculative errors were his own.

Modern Corruption

Origen's allegorical method was the original corruption: the transfer of interpretive authority from the text's plain sense to the interpreter's spiritual sensibility. Modern liberal theology's spiritualization of the Scriptures and the charismatic “deeper meaning” traditions are heirs of this approach, however remotely.

expand to see more

Origen's allegorical hermeneutic is not a postmodern corruption of his method; it IS his method, and it is the problem. He genuinely believed that the Holy Spirit had deposited deeper spiritual meanings in the text beyond and behind the literal sense, and that the spiritually advanced interpreter could access these meanings. This confidence in the interpreter's spiritual access to hidden textual meanings is the original form of what became, in liberal Protestant hermeneutics, the claim that the scholar's historical-critical reconstruction of the text's “real meaning” supersedes its surface sense, and in charismatic practice, the claim that the Spirit gives the believer direct access to a “word from the Lord” embedded in but not constrained by the text's words. The Reformation's grammatical-historical method was in part a correction of Origen's allegorism: sola scriptura meant the text's own plain meaning, not the interpreter's spiritualized construction.

Universal restoration (apokatastasis) is Origen's most consequential doctrinal error and the one most directly relevant to contemporary theology. The claim that God will ultimately restore all rational creatures — including Satan and the demons — to their original pristine state violates the explicit teaching of Matthew 25:41–46 (eternal fire for the devil and his angels; eternal punishment for the wicked) and Revelation 20:10 (the devil cast into the lake of fire and tormented day and night forever and ever). The doctrine has been revived under the label “universal reconciliation” or “Christian universalism” by writers like Robin Parry (The Evangelical Universalist) and David Bentley Hart (That All Shall Be Saved). The Reformed answer is the same as Constantinople II's: the teaching is condemned, and the condemnation is biblical.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek Origén&275;s; Alexandrian Jewish-Hellenistic intellectual tradition (Philo) as hermeneutical background; founder of systematic Christian biblical commentary and theology; the three-sense allegorical method; condemned for apokatastasis and subordinationism at Constantinople II (553 AD).

expand to see more

Alexandrian School — the intellectual context that shaped Origen; Alexandria was the meeting point of Greek philosophy (Platonism, Stoicism), Jewish allegorical interpretation (Philo), and early Christianity; Origen inherited and transformed this tradition into the first systematic Christian biblical-theological synthesis, at the cost of excessive philosophical contamination

Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BC – 50 AD) — the Jewish philosopher who pioneered the allegorical interpretation of the Hebrew Scriptures in Greek philosophical categories; Philo is the direct precedent for Origen's method; where Philo allegorized Torah, Origen allegorized the entire canon

Three-sense hermeneutic (literal, moral, allegorical) — Origen systematized his method in On First Principles 4: the literal sense (for beginners), the moral sense (for the advancing), and the allegorical or spiritual sense (for the perfect); this hierarchy privileged the allegorical and enabled speculation unbound by the text's plain meaning

Apokatastasis (αποκατάστασις) — restoration to original state; Origen's doctrine that all rational beings, having fallen from their original condition as pure minds, will eventually return to it through God's patient educative work; Acts 3:21's “restoration of all things” was one proof-text, misread from its eschatological context; the doctrine is condemned

Martyrdom and suffering — Origen's father was martyred; he himself was arrested, tortured during the Decian persecution (249–251 AD), and died from his injuries; his willingness to suffer for the faith is not in question; his theological errors proceeded from intellectual adventurism, not moral failure

Usage

"The Reformed tradition's grammatical-historical hermeneutic is partly defined against Origen's allegorism. When Calvin insists that the literal sense is the true sense and that allegory is a corruption of biblical interpretation, he is responding to a tradition that Origen founded and the medieval church perpetuated. Preaching and teaching that imports “hidden meanings,” “deeper spiritual layers,” or “what the Spirit is really saying behind the text” is methodologically Origenist, regardless of whether the preacher has read Origen. The discipline of staying with the text's own plain sense — its grammar, its context, its genre, its canonical connections — is the Reformation correction of this tendency."

"The revival of universal restoration theology in contemporary mainline and post-evangelical circles requires a clear doctrinal response. The arguments have not changed substantively since Origen: God's love is unlimited; ultimate divine victory cannot be reconciled with eternal conscious torment of rational creatures; the language of “eternal” in Matthew 25 may mean an age rather than eternity. The Reformed answer is the same as the ecumenical councils': the texts are unambiguous (Matt 25:41–46; Rev 20:10–15; Mark 9:47–48), and the doctrine contradicts the justice of God, the seriousness of sin, and the evangelistic urgency that the Gospel requires."

"Origen's case illustrates the principle that brilliant exegetical and theological ability is not self-correcting: the most intellectually formidable theologian of the third century produced the most consequential theological errors. Intellectual gifts require confessional accountability: the rule of faith, the apostolic tradition, and the gathered judgment of the church's ordained teachers are the guardrails that prevent individual genius from departing into speculation. This is the function the Reformed confessions perform: they constrain the individual teacher to the community's doctrinal inheritance."
